summary:
**ASTRA (Astronaut Self-health Tracking & Risk Assessment)** is a health-monitoring and decision-support platform designed to support astronaut wellbeing during long-duration space missions.

The platform brings together multiple aspects of astronaut health, monitoring 25 health indicators across 10 body-system domains, alongside environmental conditions and NASA’s five identified spaceflight hazards. It features an interactive health dashboard, detailed body map, personal health profiles, trend analysis, risk alerts, mission timelines and environmental monitoring. It also includes personalised countermeasure recommendations, scenario modelling, emergency-response guidance, medical inventory tracking and communication tools for situations where contact with Earth is delayed.

ASTRA addresses the challenge by helping astronauts identify potential health changes, understand developing patterns and make more informed decisions with limited access to immediate medical support. Its analytical tools compare readings against individual baselines and highlight trends that may require attention.

As missions extend towards the Moon and Mars, continuous health awareness and timely decision-making become increasingly important. ASTRA explores how an integrated, onboard system could help astronauts monitor their wellbeing and support safer, more sustainable long-duration space exploration.
details:
ASTRA – Astronaut Self-health Tracking & Risk Assessment

Project Overview

ASTRA is an astronaut health-monitoring and medical decision-support platform designed to address the challenges of maintaining crew health during long-duration space missions. Astronauts face several health risks, including space radiation, altered gravity, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, and exposure to hostile spacecraft environments. These conditions can lead to cardiovascular changes, muscle and bone loss, sleep disturbances, immune changes, cognitive impairment and other health complications.

ASTRA brings health monitoring, risk assessment and medical support together in a single platform, allowing astronauts to monitor their physiological and psychological wellbeing, identify concerning patterns and access relevant medical guidance while in space.

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

ASTRA provides an integrated monitoring system with 18 interconnected modules. It tracks 25 health indicators across 10 major body systems, covering cardiovascular, respiratory, immune, neurological, musculoskeletal, digestive, vestibular, ocular and other health functions.

Astronauts can record daily health measurements through the health scan interface, while the platform compares readings against individual pre-flight baselines and reference ranges. Its analytical engine identifies unusual changes, correlations and combinations of indicators that may suggest developing health concerns.

The platform includes:

  • An interactive anatomical body map displaying the status of different body systems.
  • Health analytics and trend visualisation to monitor changes over time.
  • A five-hazard monitoring system connecting NASA's major spaceflight hazards to potential health effects.
  • Environmental monitoring for cabin conditions such as carbon dioxide, oxygen, humidity, temperature and radiation.
  • An astronaut digital twin providing an individualised representation of health status and risk patterns.
  • Medical intelligence that helps interpret changes and suggests relevant assessments.
  • Emergency response procedures, medical inventory management and just-in-time medical training.
  • A countermeasure and recovery module to track interventions and evaluate their effectiveness.
  • Earth communication tools that generate structured medical reports while accounting for communication delays.

2. What benefits does it have?

ASTRA provides several benefits for long-duration missions. It consolidates health information that would otherwise need to be monitored across separate systems. By using individual physiological baselines, it can identify changes that may be overlooked when relying only on general medical reference ranges.

It also helps astronauts understand the relationship between their health and mission conditions. For example, changes in sleep, fatigue, heart rate and cognitive performance can be examined together rather than as isolated measurements.

Its offline decision-support design is particularly valuable for deep-space missions, where communication delays can prevent astronauts from receiving immediate assistance from Earth. The emergency response and medical training modules also help crews access organised procedures and check available medical equipment.

3. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact of ASTRA is to improve astronaut health awareness, early risk identification and medical preparedness during long-duration spaceflight.

As humanity moves towards longer lunar missions and eventual crewed Mars exploration, astronauts will need to take greater responsibility for monitoring and managing their own health. ASTRA aims to support this transition by providing an integrated platform for continuous health assessment and onboard medical decision support.

Ultimately, the project aims to contribute towards safer and more sustainable human space exploration by helping crews recognise potential health concerns earlier and make better-informed decisions when immediate ground support is unavailable.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used?

ASTRA was developed as a standalone, browser-based web application using:

  • HTML5: Application structure and content.
  • CSS3: Interface design, responsive layouts, styling and visualisation.
  • JavaScript: Health data management, analytical calculations, pattern detection, risk assessment, interactive modules and application logic.
  • SVG: Interactive anatomical body maps, charts, diagrams and visual indicators.
  • Browser Local Storage: Local persistence of user-entered measurements, completed actions, inventory changes and medical reports.

The application uses locally executed, deterministic analytical and rule-based decision-support logic. It does not currently require an external server or live internet connection for its demonstration functionality.

No physical hardware or live wearable sensors are connected in the current prototype. Health measurements and environmental readings are simulated or manually entered.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

ASTRA goes beyond a conventional health dashboard by connecting individual health indicators, environmental conditions, spaceflight hazards and medical interventions.

One of its distinctive features is the astronaut digital twin, which creates an individualised, evidence-informed representation of an astronaut's health using personal baselines, recorded measurements and mission exposures.

Another innovative feature is its interconnected risk-monitoring approach. Rather than examining symptoms independently, ASTRA identifies combinations of changes across different body systems. Its mission replay functionality also allows users to revisit the mission day by day and observe how health patterns and alerts develop over time.

The integration of emergency protocols, medical inventory, just-in-time training and delayed Earth communication makes ASTRA particularly relevant to the practical challenges of autonomous medical care in deep space.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The development of ASTRA considered several important factors:

  • Mission duration: Health changes can develop gradually over months, requiring continuous monitoring rather than occasional assessments.
  • Individual differences: Each astronaut has a different physiological baseline, so assessments should account for personal variations.
  • Spaceflight hazards: Radiation, microgravity, isolation, communication delays and spacecraft environmental conditions must be considered together.
  • Communication limitations: Essential monitoring and decision-support functions must remain available without immediate communication with Earth.
  • Medical resources: Recommendations and emergency procedures should account for the equipment, medications and consumables actually available onboard.
  • Data reliability: The platform distinguishes real reference information, simulated readings, user inputs, derived values and predicted values.
  • Privacy and accessibility: Personal health information should be appropriately protected, and the interface should remain understandable and accessible to crew members.

Data and prototype limitations: The current demonstration uses fictional astronaut profiles, fictional mission scenarios and simulated health and environmental readings. Published NASA research and reference material inform the health ranges and hazard relationships, but the displayed individual measurements are not actual astronaut medical records. ASTRA is a demonstration decision-support prototype and is not a clinically validated diagnostic system.
